source.title: Intrinsic Structure: Spectral Identifiability for Mechanistic Interpretability

record.file_problem: Readable full text; it contains some typesetting and extraction artifacts, but no material cut-off is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study argues that SAE feature dictionaries are not identifiable when their objective omits Koopman invariance, and reports a direct cross-seed feature-agreement result under an invariance-penalty intervention. It challenges or qualifies the claim that SAE features are stable canonical units, but does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The study also reports SAE invariance residuals and split-half spectral distances, but these measure dynamical closure or the reproducibility of fitted spectra, not whether SAE features are complete canonical units. Claims about SAE variability cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: Corollary 9.5 argues that reconstruction-plus-sparsity SAE dictionaries are non-identifiable, because the objective never enforces Koopman invariance. Section 11.6 measures cross-seed dictionary agreement for standard TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small, which bears directly on V5's stability and canonicality claim. The other SAE measurements (invariance residual, spectral split-half distance) concern dynamical closure or spectrum reproducibility, not feature identity.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAE run-to-run variability is structural, because the objective omits Koopman invariance. Their invariance penalty reduces spectral split-half distance by 41% (TopK), but degrades reconstruction and cross-seed feature agreement, so they do not present it as a remedy for feature-level variability. The paper's main thesis is that the identifiable Koopman spectrum is not a legible decomposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a Koopman/EDMDc spectral-realisation framework and an invariance-penalty experiment on SAEs; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE invariance ordering depends on the feature-selection rule; the paper says it reverses under variance-based selection. In the penalty experiment, results also depend on SAE architecture and penalty weight.

fits_no_version.finding: Frequency-selected SAE latents have a larger Koopman invariance residual than spectral and random dictionaries (2.1–3.4× the spectral residual). The ordering reverses under variance-based latent selection (0.70×).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionaries fail dynamical (Koopman) closure across layers, depending on the feature-selection rule.

fits_no_version.finding: Koopman spectra fitted through SAE dictionaries are less reproducible across disjoint calibration draws than spectra from spectral dictionaries, in 8 of 9 layers (factors 1.1–5.7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectra derived from SAE dictionaries are less reproducible across calibration samples.

record.problems: The feature-agreement result is limited to one model, layer, SAE architecture, width, and three seeds; uncertainty for the cosine-similarity comparison is not stated. The paper also says the penalty can degrade reconstruction and cause feature collapse at high weight.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded SAE invariance-residual comparisons and split-half spectral-distance results because they measure Koopman closure or spectrum reproducibility, not feature completeness or canonical feature identity (Sections 11.5–11.6).

missing.what: A clean row for plain TopK SAE cross-seed feature agreement (0.526 mean max cosine similarity, 3 seeds), separate from the penalty comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. Its main subject is Koopman spectral identifiability, and the SAE material is secondary. Cross-seed SAE variability cited from other work ([20–22]) is not counted as a result of this study.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure or feature importance explains polysemantic neurons or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or are evidence for superposition.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or sparse features can be recovered from LLM activations as claimed.
The study measures cross-seed feature agreement in one GPT-2 small TopK SAE setting; it does not establish feature completeness or canonicality across models, widths, layers, or training procedures.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Train TopK SAEs with the Koopman-invariance penalty at the stated penalty weight; compare cross-seed feature agreement.
rows.measure: Mean maximum cosine similarity between dictionaries from different seeds
rows.note: The authors say cross-seed feature agreement moves in the wrong direction: it decreases when the invariance penalty is raised from γ = 0 to γ = 1. This is a direct but limited measure of feature-dictionary agreement, not a completeness test.
rows.check: As recorded, the row compares the paper's own invariance-penalty method (γ=1) against plain SAEs (γ=0). That is a method comparison and is not V5 evidence. The V5-relevant value is the plain-SAE baseline: mean max cosine similarity of 0.526 across three seeds at γ=0 (TopK, layer 8, width 3072, L0=32). This means features are only partly shared across seeds. The row should be restated with subject 'standard TopK SAE (γ=0)', value 0.526, and no penalty baseline. The drop to 0.428 under the penalty should become a note or be dropped. No uncertainty or random-dictionary reference is given.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 small layer 8, TopK SAE, width 3072, L0=32, three seeds, standard objective (γ=0)
relationships.reason: Cross-seed mean max cosine similarity is only 0.526, so dictionaries are far from identical across seeds. The authors also argue theoretically (Cor. 9.5) that this variability is structural (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-seed mean max cosine similarity was only 0.526, so dictionaries were far from identical, and the authors argue theoretically that this variability is structural.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
